slides.title: A Pyramid for Weighing Evidence
bullets: In vitro and animal studies generate hypotheses, not proof in humans
Case series and observational studies show real-world associations without full confounder control
Randomized controlled trials are the standard for establishing causality
Systematic reviews and meta-analyses sit at the top, combining multiple RCTs

slides.title: Not All Evidence Carries Equal Weight
bullets: The hierarchy lets an MSL answer how strong is this evidence honestly
An observational association can be genuinely useful without proving causality
Treating both levels as equally strong is a scientific and ethical error

slides.title: The Ladder Is Not Rigid
bullets: Not every systematic review outranks a single well-designed RCT
Review quality depends on which studies were included and how they were combined
A small RCT with a wide confidence interval can be less certain than a large, well-controlled observational study
Recent methodology treats the hierarchy as a flexible guide, not a strict ladder

slides.title: Critical Appraisal Still Comes First
bullets: Design, sample size, risk of bias and clinical relevance must be weighed alongside pyramid level
Propensity score matching and other advanced methods can strengthen observational evidence
A high position in the hierarchy is a starting point, not a final verdict

slides.title: Prioritize What Deserves a Close Read
bullets: Use the hierarchy to triage the flood of available scientific literature
A recent high-impact meta-analysis deserves more attention than an isolated case report
Match language to design: association for observational data, effect only when design supports it
Anticipate design questions from critical HCPs before they ask them

slides.title: Precision Builds Trust
bullets: The hierarchy is the shared language between MSLs and the medical community
Speaking it precisely builds scientific credibility
Using it selectively to reinforce a commercial message erodes that trust

takeaway.title: The hierarchy of evidence tells an MSL how much weight to give any single data point
bullets: Randomization is what separates RCTs from studies that only show association
Meta-analyses sit at the top but still require critical appraisal, not blind trust
Matching your language to the study design keeps scientific communication honest
